definition: Kind and wanting to do good for other people.
example: The benevolent landlord lowered the rent for tenants who had recently lost their jobs.
nuance: Benevolent describes a kind intention behind an action; beneficial describes a good effect, whether or not anyone meant it.
prompt: A retired teacher spends her weekends helping out at the town library.
options: The benevolent retiree tutored young readers on weekends without asking for payment.
The benevolent retiree laughed loudly at the children who stumbled over long words in their books.
The new benevolent carpet made the library's reading room much quieter.
The doctor told the retiree that the small lump on her wrist was benevolent and nothing to fear.
reasons: Giving time freely to help children shows real goodwill toward others.
Mocking struggling kids is cruel, the reverse of kindly intent.
A carpet can be useful but has no intentions; the speaker means beneficial.
A harmless growth is benign; this word describes kind people, not medical findings.

practice.prompt: A bakery owner decides what to do with her unsold bread at closing time each night.
options: The benevolent oven baked every loaf evenly in under an hour.
The benevolent baker was known mainly for owning three shops and a large house.
Being benevolent, the baker gave her leftover loaves to the shelter down the street.
The benevolent baker threw the extra loaves in the trash so that no one else could have them.
reasons: An oven can work well, but it cannot wish anyone good.
Wealth alone says nothing about whether someone is kind to others.
Donating food to people in need is an act of goodwill.
Wasting food out of spite shows ill will, not kindness.
